record.context_brief: On the number of di ﬀerent squares in a ﬁnite word
record.original_question: (Square conjecture, due to A.S. Fraenkel and J. Simpson, [27]): The number of different squares in a word of length n is bounded by n.

evidence.quote: (Square conjecture, due to A.S. Fraenkel and J. Simpson, [27]): The number of different squares in a word of length n is bounded by n.

artifact.self_contained_problem: Let w be a finite word of length n over a finite alphabet. A square in w is a nonempty factor of the form uu (the concatenation of a word u with itself). Two squares are considered the same if they are equal as words (i.e., we count distinct square factors, not distinct occurrences). Prove or disprove: the number of distinct squares occurring as factors of w is at most n.
artifact.status_search_result: The Fraenkel–Simpson conjecture (1998) on the number of distinct squares in a word of length n has been resolved. Brlek and Li (arXiv:2204.10204, 2022) established that the number of distinct squares in a word w is at most |w| − |Alphabet(w)| + 1, which implies the conjectured bound of n. Earlier partial results gave bounds such as 2n (Fraenkel–Simpson) and below 1.5n (Thierry, 2020).

status_evidence.title: On the number of squares in a finite word
status_evidence.snippet: The number of distinct square factors of a word w is bounded by |w|-|Alphabet(w)|+1, answering the conjecture of Fraenkel and Simpson stated in 1998.
status_evidence.claim: Brlek and Li proved the Fraenkel–Simpson conjecture, with the stronger bound n − σ + 1.

status_evidence.title: A proof that a word of length n has less than 1.5n distinct squares
status_evidence.snippet: A proof that a word of length n has less than 1.5n distinct squares.
status_evidence.claim: Prior partial result by Thierry establishing a sub-1.5n bound before the full conjecture was proved.
